implementation_notes: The TypeScript default is nested spread over readonly-typed data: `{ ...person, home: { ...person.home, city: 'Berlin' } }` builds the new value with structural sharing, and `readonly` fields or `Readonly<T>` make an accidental in-place write a compile error. The typing is where the cost sits - `readonly` is shallow and erased at runtime, and a deep update of a readonly graph only type-checks if the helper's signature is written carefully (a mapped-type updater), which is why many teams take a typed optic library instead. Keep this form for one-off updates that the compiler can verify on its own.
pitfalls: `readonly` is shallow and erased at runtime: one `as` cast or an untyped boundary lets the original and the copy share and mutate the same nested object.
Spreading an instance drops its class: methods and accessors are lost, so code that treats the copy as the same type fails at runtime rather than at compile time.
Structural typing accepts any shape with the same fields, so a focus can be composed onto a structurally identical but semantically different path without a type error.

variants.name: monocle-ts Lens.fromProp composition
variants.implementation_notes: monocle-ts, the optics library of the fp-ts ecosystem, makes the focus explicit and typed: `Lens.fromProp<Employee>()('company')` builds a lens per property, `compose` chains them into one deep focus, and `Lens.fromPath` derives the same optic from a path array when the per-field boilerplate is not wanted. `modify`/`set` return the updated immutable value, so the copy cascade disappears from the call site. Adopt it when paths are data, shared across modules or derived generically; for a single nested update in one function, the spread literal is shorter and has no dependency.
pitfalls: Curried setters return a function when the value argument is forgotten, so the mistake surfaces as a type error far from the call or, with `any` in the chain, as a silent no-op.

`Lens.fromProp` does not check that the property is writable in the type sense - it copies the object, so updating a getter-only or prototype-backed property produces a value that diverges from the class's own behaviour.
The library returns new objects along the path but copies the rest by reference, so deep mutation of a sibling subtree still affects both versions.
